name: Learn Linux TV
shortDescription: A Linux and system-administration channel whose self-hosting guides start from an empty server, with separate step-by-step builds for Docker, Nextcloud, TrueNAS and Tailscale.
longDescription: Learn Linux TV is a Linux and system-administration channel whose host introduces himself as Jay and states over twenty years of Linux and sysadmin experience. Self-hosting is a minority of the catalogue, but it is the part built for someone with nothing running yet: separate walkthroughs for installing Docker and starting a first container, building Nextcloud on Debian from scratch, TrueNAS Scale, and Tailscale, plus a numbered multi-part series on server monitoring. {{longCountWords|cap}} of the {{scannedWords}} most recent uploads run past twenty minutes, with a median of {{medianPhrase}}, and the format is a screen-recorded walkthrough with time codes rather than a talk to camera. Some tutorials are paid for by the company whose product they teach, disclosed in the description each time.
notFor: Anyone after a homelab hardware channel, or a single ordered curriculum — the self-hosting material is scattered through a much larger Linux catalogue and has to be picked out by title.

categories.why: Starts from an empty machine — installing the container runtime and getting one service up — where the category's other two creators assume storage and networking are already configured.
categories.evidence: Step-by-step self-hosting builds that begin at an empty server: a Docker install-and-first-container walkthrough, Nextcloud on Debian from scratch, TrueNAS Scale, and a numbered multi-part series on server monitoring.

entryVideo.title: Easily Install Docker on Linux and Run Your First Container
entryVideo.whyThisOne: The exact step this category was missing: putting the runtime on a machine with nothing on it and getting one container running. It is also sponsor-free, which several of the channel's other build guides are not.

caveats: Some tutorials are sponsored by the company whose product they teach — Teleport, Kestra, Icinga, ThinLinc, RamNode and Tailscale among them — and although each says so in its own description, treat those recommendations as advertising rather than assessment. Every description also carries a standing block promoting the host's own courses, book and paid assistance; that block is boilerplate rather than per-video selling. The video listed here carries no sponsorship.

name: techTFQ (Thoufiq)
shortDescription: A channel that is almost entirely SQL, teaching query writing from the first SELECT through window functions and recursion, with downloadable practice data for each lesson.
longDescription: Thoufiq's channel is unusually narrow for its size: nearly every long-form upload is about SQL, database concepts or data modelling, and the beginner end is fully built out rather than implied. There are separate lessons on what a database is, writing a first query, and a two-part tutorial on joins that works through inner, left, right, full outer, cross, natural and self joins with queries on screen. The upper end is real too — window functions with frame clauses, recursive queries, GROUPING SETS against ROLLUP and CUBE. {{longCountWords|cap}} of the {{scannedWords}} most recent uploads run past twenty minutes, with a median of {{medianPhrase}}, and each lesson links downloadable scripts and datasets so the queries can be run rather than watched. He also sells a SQL practice platform and live bootcamps, promoted in every description.
notFor: Anyone wanting database internals or performance engineering — this is about writing SQL, not about how the engine executes it. The pace is deliberate and repeats itself, which is slow going if you already write queries.

categories.why: Teaches the first query and the first join as their own lessons, where the category's other two creators start at internals and performance and assume you can already write SQL.
categories.evidence: A catalogue in which nearly every long-form upload is SQL: separate tutorials on what a database is, SQL basics with practice queries, and a two-part joins series covering inner, left, right, full outer, cross, natural and self joins, each with downloadable scripts and datasets.

entryVideo.title: SQL Basics Tutorial for Beginners (Practice SQL Queries)
entryVideo.whyThisOne: Starts at writing a first query rather than at schema design or tuning, and the practice queries are downloadable so you can type them rather than watch them. It carries no sponsorship, which the channel's more recent beginner course does.

caveats: Sells a SQL practice platform and live bootcamps of his own, linked from every description — treat the recommendations to buy them as advertising. Roughly one long-form upload in ten carries a third-party sponsorship, in each case for an unrelated product such as Skillshare or Brilliant rather than for a database tool, and the video listed here carries none. Several videos are five or six years old; SQL syntax has not moved, but the surrounding tooling shots have.

name: Simple Snippets (Tanmay Sakpal)
shortDescription: Diagram-led computer-science teaching whose data-structures videos ask what each structure is for before showing any code.
longDescription: Simple Snippets is a broad computer-science teaching channel — its own description lists programming, databases, networking, computer architecture, operating systems and mathematics — and roughly half its long-form output is data structures. The distinguishing habit is in the titles: "What is HASHING? Why do we NEED it?", "What is Balancing a binary tree and why do we need balancing", "What is Infix Prefix & Postfix Expressions in Data Structures | Why do we need them?". Each one names the problem the structure solves before the structure, which is the opposite order from interview-pattern teaching. Explanations are built on hand-drawn diagrams with code following afterwards rather than leading. {{longCountWords|cap}} of the {{scannedWords}} most recent uploads run past twenty minutes, with a median of {{medianPhrase}}.
notFor: Anyone drilling for interviews or contests — there are no pattern catalogues or timed problem sets here, and the pace assumes you want the concept rather than the trick. Recent uploads have moved to computer graphics and competitive programming, so the data-structures material is a back catalogue rather than something still growing.

categories.why: Asks what problem each structure solves before showing it, where the category's other two creators start from interview patterns and contest technique and assume you already know why a hash table exists.
categories.evidence: Roughly half the long-form catalogue is data structures, built around explicitly comparative explanations — hashing introduced as array against hash table, trees against graphs, balanced against unbalanced — with diagrams first and code second.

entryVideo.title: What is a Tree? | Introduction to Tree Data Structure (diagram) | Important Tree Terms & Properties
entryVideo.whyThisOne: Defines a structure and its vocabulary from nothing, which is the step both existing creators skip. It carries no sponsorship, unlike the channel's hashing video.

caveats: About one long-form upload in twenty carries a sponsorship, in the cases named for Unacademy, an exam-coaching platform — none of them is the data-structures material listed here, and the entry video carries none. The channel's recent output is computer graphics and competitive programming, so the data-structures videos date from 2020 to 2023; the concepts have not moved but the on-screen tooling has.

name: Net Ninja (Shaun Pelling)
shortDescription: A long-running web-development tutorial channel whose numbered series include a fourteen-part beginner course on unit testing with Vitest.
longDescription: Net Ninja is a web-development teaching channel built almost entirely from numbered tutorial series — JavaScript, React, Node, Firebase and a long list of tools, each taught in sequential episodes with the course files on GitHub. Its unit-testing series starts from what a unit test is and why you would write one, then covers a first test, matchers, what makes a test readable, test-driven development, async code, mocks and spies, in episodes that run from a few minutes to about twenty. The channel as a whole favours short lessons: across the {{scannedWords}} most recent uploads the median is {{medianPhrase}}. The testing material is JavaScript-specific; the ideas transfer, the syntax does not.
notFor: Anyone past their first test suite — the series stops at mocks and spies and does not reach test boundaries, integration testing or how to keep a large suite fast, and outside that one series the channel is general web development rather than testing.

categories.why: Starts from what a unit test is and walks through writing the first one, where the category's other two creators assume you already test and argue about how to do it better.
categories.evidence: A fourteen-part "Unit Testing (Vitest) Tutorial" series from late 2025: what unit testing is, writing a first test, matchers, writing better tests, test-driven development, async functions, mock functions and spies.

entryVideo.title: Unit Testing (Vitest) Tutorial #1 - What is Unit Testing?
entryVideo.whyThisOne: Opens the series by explaining what a unit test checks and setting up a project to run one, so the next episode can go straight to writing it.

selection.note: The only channel we found teaching unit testing from the first test upward. The other testing channels we looked at assumed you already write tests, or taught one language's tools at an intermediate level. The series itself is squarely what a beginner needs; it is the choice around it that is thin.

caveats: Every description in the series links to the creator's own paid site, where the same course is released early and a testing bundle is sold; the YouTube episodes are complete without it. No third-party sponsorship was found in the descriptions of the 110 most recent long-form uploads. The examples are JavaScript with Vitest, so a Python or C# learner will need to translate the syntax.

name: David Taylor
shortDescription: A college writing instructor teaching the mechanics of student essays and research papers: thesis, paragraph structure, when and how to cite, and APA and MLA formatting.
longDescription: David Taylor describes himself as a college writing and communications instructor of two decades' standing, currently teaching at the University of Maryland Global Campus and Parker University. The channel is organised around what a first-year student has to produce: an essay with a thesis and body paragraphs, a research paper in APA or MLA format, citations that are neither missing nor excessive. Short explanations sit alongside recordings of his own course sessions, and the descriptions link to his own templates, sample papers and playlists. Across the {{scannedWords}} most recent uploads the median runs {{medianPhrase}}. A smaller strand teaches English grammar and test-essay technique to non-native writers.
notFor: Graduate students and anyone writing for publication — the material stops at the undergraduate paper, and about one long-form upload in six is a recorded class session for a specific nursing-college course rather than a standalone lesson.

categories.why: Teaches the first essay and the first cited paper step by step, where the category's two existing creators start at the thesis, the literature review and journal publication.
categories.evidence: Long-form lessons on writing an essay step by step, writing an APA research paper from introduction to reference list, when a source needs citing, avoiding plagiarism, and improving academic prose.

entryVideo.title: How to Write an Essay Step-by-Step | The 4-Sentence Method
entryVideo.whyThisOne: Plans an essay from a thesis statement down to each body paragraph with one repeatable outline, which is the structure a beginner needs before anything about style.

selection.note: The only active channel we found teaching a first undergraduate essay step by step. The others we looked at were study vlogs, sentence-level English for non-native writers, or channels that no longer post. The lessons themselves are on target; it is the choice around them that is thin.

caveats: His credentials are as the channel states them and were not independently confirmed. The long-form catalogue mixes standalone lessons with recorded live sessions from courses he teaches, which assume that course's assignments. No sponsorship disclosure appears in the descriptions of the 67 most recent long-form uploads; their links are labelled as his own templates, sample papers and playlists. One video walks through a free citation generator, which is a tutorial on the tool rather than an endorsement disclosed as paid.

name: Nutrition Triathlon (James LeBaigue)
shortDescription: A sports nutritionist working with amateur triathletes, explaining how much to eat, how much protein is enough and how to fuel long training and race days.
longDescription: James LeBaigue introduces himself as a sports nutritionist with an MSc who works one-to-one with amateur and professional triathletes, and the long-form covers the questions those athletes tend to start with: how much protein a triathlete needs, why calorie tracking may not be worth it, what people get wrong about fuelling, and how to carb-load and fuel a long race. His descriptions present the material as drawn from current research rather than personal advice, and the protein video pushes back on high figures promoted by prominent voices and companies. Most of the channel's recent output is short clips — {{shortPctWords}} per cent of the {{scannedWords}} most recent uploads run under two minutes — with the long-form explainers sitting between them. Everything is framed for triathlon and endurance training.
notFor: Strength and team-sport athletes looking for sport-specific plans — the examples, numbers and race scenarios are triathlon and endurance throughout, and the long-form explainers are outnumbered by short clips.

categories.why: Answers the adequacy questions a newer endurance athlete has first — total intake, protein per day, whether to track — where the category's other creators start at periodised fuelling and performance research.
categories.evidence: Long-form explainers on daily protein needs for triathletes, dropping calorie tracking, common nutrition mistakes, a complete triathlon nutrition guide, and carbohydrate loading and race fuelling for 70.3 and Ironman distances.

entryVideo.title: STOP Following Wrong Protein Advice — What Triathletes Need
entryVideo.whyThisOne: Works out how much protein an endurance athlete needs per day, set against the higher figures promoted by prominent voices and companies — the adequacy question the beginner level starts from.

selection.note: The best of a thin field rather than a clear choice. The other channels we found were plant-based cooking, general fitness or short clips; this one does answer the first questions about eating enough, but mostly in short clips, for triathletes, and alongside affiliate links. Searched once, with one query aimed at beginners; we would revisit this if a stronger beginner voice turned up.

caveats: His qualification is as the channel states it and was not independently confirmed. Every description promotes his own paid coaching, community and fuelling guides. Some descriptions carry affiliate links — a calorie-tracking app, running gear on Amazon, a training-software discount — and one video builds race plans entirely from a single sports-nutrition brand's products without a sponsorship disclosure; the entry video carries none of these. Two recent videos compare branded electrolyte and recovery drinks. General information rather than individual dietary advice, as his own descriptions say.

name: Starting Strength
shortDescription: The channel of the Starting Strength method: coaching videos on the squat, deadlift, press and bench press, and a simple novice linear progression for someone who has never lifted.
longDescription: Starting Strength is a single named method — five barbell lifts, each taught through its own set progression, and a novice linear progression to run them in — and this channel is its video arm, alongside the method's own coaches and affiliated gyms. The teaching sits in the back catalogue: Mark Rippetoe coaching the squat, deadlift, press and bench press on lifters of varying size and build, taken from the method's 2010 instructional DVD, then shorter coach-led explanations of common errors and of how to run the first month of the progression. The recent output is mostly clipped previews from the Starting Strength Network, and {{shortPctWords}} per cent of the {{scannedWords}} most recent uploads are under two minutes. A beginner who wants one coherent answer rather than a survey of options will find it here.
notFor: Anyone who wants several approaches weighed against each other — everything here is taught as the one correct way, and the recent uploads are podcast clips rather than lessons, so the useful material has to be found in the older catalogue.

categories.why: Teaches the first four barbell lifts from nothing and a novice programme you can run the next day, where the category's other creators start at periodisation, autoregulation and training blocks.
categories.evidence: Full coaching videos for the squat, deadlift, bench press and press with Mark Rippetoe, later coach-led videos on fixing common deadlift and press errors, and explainers on running the novice linear progression through its first month.

entryVideo.title: The Novice Linear Progression: Your First 30 Days
entryVideo.whyThisOne: Lays out how to run the first month of a simple progression on your own — what to lift, how to add weight, what to expect — which is the whole of the beginner level in eleven minutes.

caveats: This is a commercial method with its own coaches, gyms and network, and every description links to them; no third-party sponsorship appears in the descriptions of the 45 most recent long-form uploads, and the entry video carries none. The method is presented as the right way rather than one way, so read it alongside the category's critic. Three specific positions on the channel run against mainstream evidence: rating how hard a set felt (RPE) is dismissed as useless, where this category's intermediate level recommends learning exactly that; a gallon of milk a day is advised for lifters trying to gain weight; and a guest episode argues that the medical consensus on cholesterol and heart disease is wrong. Fewer than one upload in fifty, by title, turns to politics, medicine or hormone therapy rather than training.

name: The Finance Storyteller (Philip de Vroe)
shortDescription: A finance trainer who explains the income statement, balance sheet, cash flow statement and common ratios by walking through the published accounts of real companies.
longDescription: Philip de Vroe runs finance training through classroom sessions and webinars as well as this channel, and the channel's method is consistent: take one real company's published statements — Microsoft, Walmart, Airbus, Uber — and read them line by line, naming each item and what it tells you. The core set covers each of the three financial statements separately, how to read all three together, and single ratios such as price-to-earnings and the current ratio, each explained on actual figures. Descriptions carry the full written explanation and timestamps, so a video can be followed as a text afterwards. Across the {{scannedWords}} most recent uploads the median runs {{medianPhrase}}, with short clips mixed in.
notFor: Anyone looking for stock picks, a valuation model or an investing strategy — the channel teaches how to read accounts and what the numbers mean, and stops before telling you what to buy or whether you can beat the market.

categories.why: Teaches how to read the three financial statements and the common ratios on real companies' accounts, the step the category's two existing creators take for granted before they start valuing a business.
categories.evidence: Separate explainers on the income statement, the balance sheet and reading all three statements together, ratio explainers for price-to-earnings and the current ratio, and a full analysis of a company's quarterly results, each built on a named company's published figures.

entryVideo.title: How to read financial statements
entryVideo.whyThisOne: Reads Microsoft's income statement, balance sheet and cash flow statement for one year in turn and shows how they connect, which is the whole of the beginner level applied to a real company.

caveats: The channel invites paid YouTube channel memberships for bonus content; no third-party sponsorship or affiliate placement appears in the descriptions of the 73 most recent long-form uploads, and the entry video carries none. Some of the core explainers date from 2018 to 2020 and use those years' figures; the method has not changed but the numbers have.

name: Dr Brad Stanfield
shortDescription: A New Zealand GP summarising recent trials on blood pressure, exercise, sleep, cholesterol and supplements for people who want to age well, with the papers linked under every video.
longDescription: Brad Stanfield is a primary care physician in New Zealand, and the channel turns new studies and guideline changes into short explainers on what they mean for someone trying to stay healthy for longer. Much of it is the unglamorous core — blood pressure targets, how much exercise and of what kind, sleep, cholesterol and statins — alongside debunkings of anti-ageing products and a steady strand on supplements. Each description lists the research papers the video draws on, and the credits name a separate scriptwriter and editor. Across the {{scannedWords}} most recent uploads the median runs {{medianPhrase}}.
notFor: Anyone who wants the biology of ageing or the frontier of longevity research — this is a clinician's reading of trials for everyday decisions, and the supplement coverage sits beside a supplement the channel sells.

categories.why: Covers the established interventions — blood pressure, exercise, sleep — as practical explainers built on current trials, where every creator already in the category is pitched at intermediate and advanced.
categories.evidence: Recurring explainers on blood pressure targets and lowering it without medication, the best exercise for blood pressure and for longevity, fitting exercise into a busy week, sleep quality, and cholesterol and statins, each description listing the studies cited.

entryVideo.title: Naturally Lower YOUR Blood Pressure
entryVideo.whyThisOne: Goes through the lifestyle measures with trial evidence for lowering blood pressure, one of the well-established levers the beginner level starts from, and its description lists sixteen sources and no products.

selection.note: The best of a thin field rather than a clear choice. The other channels we found dealt mainly in experimental anti-ageing interventions, ageing-biology research or multi-hour interviews; this one covers the established basics, but it also sells a supplement while advising on supplements. Searched once, with one query aimed at beginners; we would revisit this if a beginner voice without that conflict turned up.

caveats: The channel sells its own multivitamin, linked from several 2025 videos, and from 2020 to 2023 over a hundred descriptions carried personal discount codes for three supplement retailers — while supplements are a regular topic of the videos. That is a direct commercial interest in one of the decisions the channel advises on; weigh the supplement videos accordingly. The blood-pressure, exercise and sleep material, including the entry video, links research papers rather than products. Every description carries a standing affiliate notice whether or not it contains product links. His medical registration is linked from the channel and was not independently checked. General information, not individual medical advice, as the channel itself says.

name: House of Hypertrophy
shortDescription: Research reviews on the core training variables of building muscle — sets, reps, protein, exercise choice, what muscle growth actually is — with every study listed underneath.
longDescription: House of Hypertrophy describes itself simply as research-backed videos on muscle and strength gain, and the format holds throughout: take one practical question, walk through the meta-analyses and individual trials that bear on it, then say what the evidence does and does not settle. The recurring questions are the core training variables — sets per muscle, rep ranges, protein intake, training frequency — answered for someone who wants the literature rather than a rule of thumb, alongside long single-muscle guides such as a fifty-minute one on the chest. Most long-form descriptions carry timestamps and a reference list, often a dozen or more studies. Across the {{scannedWords}} most recent uploads the median runs {{medianPhrase}}.
notFor: Someone who has never trained and wants to be told where to start — there is no programme, routine or starting-out video in the catalogue, and the study-by-study pace suits a lifter who already trains and wants the reasoning behind the variables they are adjusting.

categories.why: Weighs each training variable — weekly sets, rep ranges, protein — against the published studies one question at a time, a narrower and more literature-bound treatment than the category's programming-focused creators give.
categories.evidence: Evidence reviews on weekly sets per muscle, rep ranges for growth, protein requirements while bulking and cutting, the best exercises for hypertrophy, and what physically happens inside a muscle as it grows, each with its reference list in the description.

entryVideo.title: The Science of What Muscle Growth Actually Is
entryVideo.whyThisOne: Explains what physically gets bigger when a muscle grows and how settled each mechanism is, which is the model the channel's later reviews of sets, reps and protein build on; its description carries references and music credits and no product links.

caveats: Since 2023 most descriptions open with a personalised link to a third-party workout-tracking app, with no statement of whether it is paid; the entry video predates this and carries none. The channel does not name the person presenting it.

name: David Travis
shortDescription: Short answers from a UX researcher to the practical questions of running user research: how to moderate a usability test, how to choose participants, which methods to trust.
longDescription: David Travis describes himself as a user experience strategist at the consultancy Userfocus and the author of three books, the latest on thinking like a UX researcher. The channel is a finished set of five-minute answers to single questions — which usability testing method to choose, a moderation checklist, how to take notes in a test, how to pick participants, how to avoid bias — plus a six-part series on how researchers think. Several take a clear position against common practice, arguing for example that focus groups and preference testing mislead more than they inform. Across the {{scannedWords}} uploads scanned the median runs {{medianPhrase}}.
notFor: Anyone wanting to see a design made — this is research method, not interface design, and nobody opens a design file here; and anyone wanting current tooling, since the channel stopped in 2020.

categories.why: Answers the practical questions of running usability tests and user research one at a time, from a working consultant, where the category's other creator publishes research summaries as an institution.
categories.evidence: Around sixty short videos on user research practice — choosing a usability testing method, a test moderation checklist, note taking in tests, choosing participants, avoiding bias, field visits against surveys — and a six-part series on how UX researchers think.

entryVideo.title: UX Tea Break: Usability Test Moderation Checklist
entryVideo.whyThisOne: Walks through what to do before, during and after moderating a usability test, with a checklist to download, which is the step between having a design and watching a real person use it.

caveats: The channel has not posted since December 2020; the methods have not changed but anything about tools or the job market has. Every description lists his paid training courses and book. He works from the same research-first position as the category's other creator, so the two agree more than they differ — neither is a designer showing interface work from start to finish, which is the view this category still lacks.

name: Dr. Maika Steinborn
shortDescription: A clinical psychologist explaining attachment patterns in adult relationships — what each style does and does not describe, and how anxious and avoidant partners set each other off.
longDescription: Maika Steinborn describes herself as a clinical and educational psychologist, and a steady share of her long-form work is attachment in adult relationships. The videos work at the level of behaviour: what an avoidant shutdown is and what is happening underneath it, how to answer an anxiously attached partner's implicit accusations, how two insecure styles escalate each other, and what securely attached people do differently in conflict. Several push directly against reading the styles as fixed types — separating avoidant attachment from an ordinary conflict response, or listing the common misreadings of avoidant people. Some are two-psychologist conversations; across the {{scannedWords}} most recent uploads the median runs {{medianPhrase}}.
notFor: Anyone after the research itself — the channel applies attachment ideas to relationships rather than examining the studies or their limits, and a few older videos use the 'signs you are' format the rest of the channel argues against.

categories.why: Works through attachment as behaviour between two people — shutdowns, accusations, how styles escalate each other — from a clinical psychologist, where the category's existing creator writes long essays on the individual mechanics of each style.
categories.evidence: Around thirty long-form videos in the most recent two hundred on adult attachment: avoidant shutdowns, supporting an anxious partner, compatibility between styles, fearful-avoidant attachment, what secure partners do in disagreement, and common misreadings of avoidant people.

entryVideo.title: Psychologist On: Do You Have Avoidant Attachment—or Just a Common Conflict Response?
entryVideo.whyThisOne: Separates what actually counts as an avoidant attachment pattern from ordinary ways of handling conflict, which is the beginner level's first lesson — what the labels describe and what they do not.

caveats: Since 2023 most descriptions open with a link to the channel's own attachment-style quiz, which leads into a paid programme for avoidant men, and both videos checked in full, the entry video among them, end with a chapter promoting that programme. A quiz that sorts you into a style is the use of the labels this category warns against, even though the videos themselves argue against treating the styles as fixed types. Her qualifications are as the channel states them and were not independently confirmed. No third-party sponsorship appears in the descriptions of the most recent long-form uploads.

name: Brian Winrow
shortDescription: A US tax attorney and university tax lecturer explaining how the federal income tax system works, from how brackets apply to your pay to deductions, credits and filing status.
longDescription: Brian Winrow describes himself as a tax attorney and educator who teaches tax and accounting, and his descriptions address accounting students, CPA and enrolled-agent candidates, and ordinary taxpayers together. The catalogue explains the system rather than giving filing tips: a beginner strand on how tax brackets actually apply, marginal against effective and average rates, whether a raise can cost you money, and reading your first pay stub; then deductions, credits, filing status and the W-4 form line by line; and full-length lectures from his introductory university tax course. Across the {{scannedWords}} most recent uploads the median runs {{medianPhrase}}, with {{longCountWords}} past twenty minutes.
notFor: Anyone outside the United States looking for their own rules, and anyone wanting a quick filing checklist — the channel teaches the reasoning behind US federal tax, some of it at university-course length, and a strand of recent videos is onboarding advice for new tax-firm staff.
jurisdictionNote: US federal income tax throughout. How brackets work and the difference between marginal and effective rates carry over to most countries; the forms, figures, deductions and credits do not.

categories.why: Explains how the US income tax system works from brackets upward, a second jurisdiction beside the category's Canadian creator, and the system rather than filing tips.
categories.evidence: A beginner series on how tax brackets apply, marginal against effective and average tax rates, whether a raise can lower take-home pay, beginner tax terms and reading a first pay stub; plus explainers on standard against itemised deductions, filing status, education credits and line-by-line W-4 walkthroughs.

entryVideo.title: Marginal vs Effective vs Average Tax Rate (How to Understand Your Real Return)
entryVideo.whyThisOne: Works through one example to show what the marginal rate on your next dollar is, what your overall tax burden is, and which of the two matters for which decision — the beginner level's first lesson.

caveats: His qualifications are as the channel states them and were not independently confirmed. Descriptions link to his own tax practice; no third-party sponsorship or software placement appears in the descriptions of the most recent long-form uploads, and the entry video carries none. Several recent videos are aimed at new staff in tax firms rather than at taxpayers.

name: William Ury
shortDescription: An archive of talks, lectures and interviews by a co-founder of the Harvard Program on Negotiation, teaching the interest-based approach to reaching agreement.
longDescription: The channel describes William Ury as an author, negotiator and mediator and a co-founder of the Harvard Program on Negotiation, and it collects his recorded appearances rather than lessons made for YouTube: book talks on getting to agreement and on getting past a refusal, a four-part lecture series, executive-education seminars, a TEDx talk, and long conversations about negotiating peace in Venezuela, the Middle East and between Russia and Ukraine. The approach is the interest-based one — look past the stated position to what each side needs, and know your walk-away alternative — which is a different school from tactical, empathy-led negotiation. Across the {{scannedWords}} uploads scanned the median runs {{medianPhrase}}, and the channel has not posted since early 2024.
notFor: Anyone wanting step-by-step lessons or a preparation checklist — these are recorded talks and interviews, about one in five running forty-five minutes or more, and a handful of uploads are in Portuguese, Spanish or Italian.

categories.why: Teaches the interest-based school of negotiation — separating what people demand from what they need, and knowing your alternative to a deal — which is a different method from the category's other creator.
categories.evidence: A four-part lecture on getting past a refusal, executive-education seminars on negotiating to win and on family-business negotiations, talks on reaching sustainable agreements from the Harvard Negotiation Project, and long discussions of multi-party diplomatic negotiations.

entryVideo.title: Getting Past No Part 1 (Spanish Subtitles)
entryVideo.whyThisOne: Opens a four-part lecture on what to do when the other side says no — staying in a hard conversation without either conceding or escalating. English audio; the subtitles in the title are Spanish.

caveats: The channel has not posted since February 2024, and it is a collection of recorded appearances rather than a course, so there is no single place to start, and about one upload in five runs forty-five minutes or more. 8 of its 99 uploads are declared in Portuguese, Spanish or Italian. His affiliations are as the channel states them and were not independently confirmed. The descriptions carry no product or sponsor links.
